content: Individuals experiencing changes in their health may require assistance in adapting how they perform daily tasks or in improving their ability to instruct others effectively. For wheelchair users with cognitive impairments, training should be adjusted to their specific needs. This may involve conducting training in the environments where the wheelchair will be used, offering shorter and more frequent sessions over an extended period, and involving familiar individuals to provide support. Training for mobility skills should be tailored to the environments in which the wheelchair will be used. Ideally, this training should occur in settings that closely resemble the user’s living or working environment. For individuals with cognitive impairments, training should be simplified and broken into smaller steps, with family or caregivers involved to reinforce learning through frequent practice. Accessible information, such as easy-to-read materials, should also be provided. Similarly, individuals with vision, hearing, or communication impairments require accessible training methods and materials. Specialized facilities for task-specific training are not always necessary, as existing spaces can often be adapted for training purposes. However, having a dedicated area can enhance focus and effectiveness. Such spaces may include indoor or outdoor areas with varied surfaces and obstacles for wheelchair mobility training, as well as environments that simulate home or work settings. Wheelchair users can practice essential tasks such as transferring in and out of the wheelchair, reaching, and working at a desk or kitchen counter. The duration, content, and frequency of training should be customized to the skills required to meet the wheelchair user’s goals and their ability to achieve competency. Follow-up care is a critical component of wheelchair service delivery and should be available to all users for as long as they require a wheelchair. Follow-up involves two key components: review and remediation. The review process includes collaboration between the wheelchair user and service provider to assess how well the wheelchair continues to meet the user’s needs, its condition, and the user’s ability to use it safely and effectively. Remediation addresses and resolves any identified issues, such as adjustments to the wheelchair, additional training, or necessary repairs. Timely follow-up is essential to prevent worsening problems and potential health or financial consequences. Clear communication between the service provider and the wheelchair user is crucial to avoid frustration and mistrust. Follow-up is not complete until both the user and the service provider are satisfied with the solutions provided. Maintenance and repair are among the most common remediation actions and are vital for ensuring the safety, health, and mobility of the wheelchair user while extending the lifespan of the equipment. Follow-up can be conducted through various methods, including telehealth, phone calls, or in-person visits, depending on the context and needs. In areas with reliable internet access, telehealth can be an effective tool for follow-up care. For example, in Argentina, a program uses telehealth to connect local health workers with remote wheelchair provision experts, enabling follow-up care even in remote regions. This approach has reduced the abandonment of wheelchairs and improved outcomes for users. While the optimal interval for follow-up appointments has not been defined, it is recommended that new wheelchair users and those with stable health conditions be followed up at least annually. Children, older adults, and individuals with rapidly changing health conditions should be followed up at least biannually. A competent workforce is essential for effective wheelchair service delivery. Personnel involved in wheelchair provision must have role-specific competencies, including clinical, technical, and management skills. Licensing and certification requirements further support the feasibility of training and competency assessment. In Bhutan, a national wheelchair service has been developed using WHO training packages and skills tests. This initiative has integrated wheelchair service training into the national physiotherapy curriculum, ensuring a sustainable and structured approach to service delivery. The involvement of wheelchair users in training and service development has been crucial for creating services that meet their needs and foster trust within the community. Strategies to strengthen the workforce include task-shifting, defining competencies, integrating wheelchair training into educational curricula, and introducing national accreditation. Task-shifting involves training personnel at primary health levels to handle basic wheelchair service steps, reserving complex cases for specialized providers. Defining core competencies and offering advanced training can address the needs of users with varying complexities. Integrating wheelchair training into health personnel curricula and introducing certification requirements can further enhance service quality and accessibility. Effective integration and networking with other services and stakeholders are essential for meeting the individualized needs of wheelchair users.
